doc.title: Larry Gold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2025

title: Telling the story with strings for hip hop artists
summary: Singers and rappers tell a story, and Gold follows the arc of the song, which he credits for his success with hip hop.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Right. It's not the way these mics are perceived or even the way — you know one of the things about great vocalists you know they might be belters you know but they'll entice you into a song. They don't start out belting. Or some of them don't, I mean Aretha sometimes did and some of these other young people like Jennifer Hudson does sometimes. But — [there's a little traffic out here, I'm sorry]. But it's more like you're telling a story and even with your voice you're telling a story. And even with the violin or the cello or the arrangement or the record, you know it's like I remember a lot of these hip hop kids when they started coming to me in the late '90s and the middle '90s whenever it started, that big wave that I had there for a while. You know they would say after I finished an arrangement they'd say, "Man, you were like telling a story with the strings." They were the one telling the story, all I was doing was following their arc.
Following their arc. I like that.

You know and even though a lot of the hip hop records started the same and ended the same, there was always like a vocal arc. You know even the rapper had to breathe. Or on some of those records the singing came into the choruses. But I would always try to follow the arc of the song, which is what I did when I was a little kid. So to me I remember you know I mean maybe I cared too much about it but I really don't think I did. I think that part of my success within the frame of hip hop was because that's what I did.
I'm not sure what you mean, that's what you did?

I told the story with the arrangement in a way as they were telling a story, depending on what — I didn't care who it was. It could be, you know The Roots or anybody. I mean I told the story. They were telling a story and I did too. So it wasn't just the same line that came in and that's what the arranging on popular music became that. It became very similar. You'd write a line for the chorus and it came in every time.
